To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
abdominal obesity and the associated metabolic syndrome are important clinical markers of global cardiometabolic risks.

the most prevalent metabolic abnormalities associated with insulin resistance are found in patients with excess visceral/ectopia fat and that a simple clinical diagnosis of visceral/ectopia obesity or the metabolic syndrome is insufficient to assess global risk for cardiovascular disease.
the presence of abdominal fat accumulation, especially visceral fat, is associated with an increased cardiometabolic risk.
In summary, our research is concerned with
defining the pathophysiological mechanisms of abdominal obesity and their contribution to the metabolic syndrome and to global cardiometabolism risk.
the metabolic consequences of abdominal obesity in humans,

the pathophysiology of visceral obesity, its role as a marker of insulin resistance, and its role in the development of the metabolic syndrome as well as the clinical implications of this constellation of abnormalities for the prediction of cardiovascular disease.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

visceral obesity and the metabolic (or cardiometabolic) syndrome are two different clinical phenotypes which share a common underlying metabolic disorder and which both represent a risk factor for cardiovascular disease.

visceral obesity and the metabolic (insulin resistance) syndrome represent a major intermediate phenotype of cardiometabolic risk, which is associated with a cluster of metabolic abnormalities including elevated triglycerides and low HDL cholesterol, hypertension, elevated fasting glucose and insulin, and elevated blood uric acid, all of these abnormalities being linked to insulin resistance, atherogenic dyslipidemia, prothrombosis, and a proinflammatory state.
abdominal obesity and visceral fat are the most important components of the metabolic syndrome which is associated with a high global cardiometabolic cardiovascular risk.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

abdominal obesity and the presence of the metabolic syndrome are associated with an increased cardiometabolic risk which is best assessed by the presence of the classical cardiovascular risk factors and of the presence of abdominal fat accumulation.

abdominal obesity, especially visceral obesity, is the main component of the "metabolic" or "insulinaemic" or "syndrome" X, but that this clinical entity is only one of the components of the global cardiometabolic cardiovascular risk.
the metabolic syndrome is a constellation of metabolic disorders that includes visceral obesity and that the cardiometabolic risk is defined as the sum of the classical and metabolic risks.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the clinical definition of the metabolic risk is not the same as that of visceral obesity, and that the latter may represent a better marker of the metabolic syndrome than the former.
visceral obesity and the metabolic should be considered as clinical markers of cardiometabolic risk.

visceral obesity, insulin sensitivity, or the metabolic syndrome are not diseases per se, but rather clinical intermediate phenotypes that are markers of the global cardiometabolic burden of a patient.
